t: Reply to tricky emails calmly and clearly
d: Paste in an awkward email and get two ready-to-send replies, one warm and one firm, that say exactly what you mean.
when: Whenever an email makes you hesitate

steps.h: Copy the email you need to answer
steps.b: Copy the message (and the one before it if it gives context). Remove phone numbers, account numbers or anything private first.

steps.h: Jot down what you actually want to say
steps.b: One or two rough lines is enough, for example 'Can't do Friday, can do next Tuesday, and I need the files first'.

steps.h: Ask your AI assistant for two versions
steps.b: Open ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini and paste this prompt with the email and your notes.
steps.p:
I need to reply to the email below. My goal: [what you want to happen]. My key points: [your rough notes]. My relationship with the sender: [e.g. client, manager, neighbour]. Write two replies under 120 words each: Version A warm and friendly, Version B polite but firm. Keep my points in the same order, use plain British English, no clichés, and end with one clear next step. Then list anything in their email I haven't answered.

Their email:
[paste email]

steps.b: Choose the version that sounds most like you, change any words you wouldn't use, and paste it into your reply.

example: Version B: Hi Sam, thanks for the update. I can't take on the extra pages by Friday, but I can deliver them by Tuesday 14th if I have the final copy by Thursday. Shall we go with that? Not yet answered: their question about invoicing.
tips: Ask it to 'make this sound more like me' and paste two emails you've sent before as a style guide.
Always read the reply aloud once before sending; tone is easier to hear than see.

trigger.detail: User selects an email and asks for help replying

actions.detail: Write a warm and a firm reply from the user's key points
Save the chosen version as a draft reply

t: Get a morning briefing of what matters in your inbox
d: Start each day with a short list of emails that need a reply, emails you can skim and anything with a deadline.
when: Every weekday morning

steps.h: Connect your AI assistant to your email
steps.b: Use Gemini in Gmail, Copilot in Outlook, or the Gmail connector in ChatGPT or Claude if your plan includes it. Check your workplace AI policy before connecting a work account.
Keep this prompt in your notes app so you can paste it each morning.
steps.p: Look at the emails I received since [yesterday at 5pm]. Give me a briefing in three sections: 1) Needs my reply today: sender, subject, what they want, in one line each. 2) Deadlines or dates mentioned: what, when, and who it's from. 3) Safe to skim or archive: grouped by type (newsletters, receipts, notifications). Ignore anything from [senders to ignore]. Keep the whole briefing under 200 words.

steps.b: Add a recurring weekday reminder at the time you start work, linking to your saved prompt.

steps.h: Use the free fallback if you can't connect
steps.b: Select the subject lines and senders from your inbox list, copy them, and paste them into your AI assistant with the same prompt.

example: Needs reply: Priya (school office) - confirm trip consent by Wed. Tom (supplier) - approve revised quote. Deadlines: Council tax direct debit changes 1 Dec. Skim: 6 newsletters, 3 delivery updates, 2 receipts.
tips: AI can miss things, so glance at your unread count once after the briefing.
Tell it which people always matter (your boss, your child's school) so they're never lumped into 'skim'.

trigger.detail: Weekdays at 8am

actions.detail: Summarise emails received since the last briefing
Sort into reply today, deadlines and skim
Send the briefing to the user

t: Sort incoming email into labels automatically
d: Get a set of email filters that file receipts, newsletters and notifications into their own labels or folders, so your inbox shows people.
when: Once, then tweak monthly

steps.b: Scroll back through a week of email and write down the senders and subject words that crowd your inbox, such as 'order', 'receipt' or a shop's name.

steps.h: Ask AI to design your filing system
steps.b: Paste your list into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: I want to tidy my [Gmail / Outlook] inbox with filters. Here are senders and subject words that clutter it: [paste list]. Suggest no more than 6 labels/folders (e.g. Receipts, Newsletters, Notifications, Travel). For each, give: the label name, the exact sender addresses or words to match, and whether it should skip the inbox or stay in it. Present it as a table I can follow one row at a time. Flag anything that might catch important personal emails by mistake.

steps.b: In Gmail, search for the senders, then choose 'Create filter' from the search options and apply a label. In Outlook, right-click a message and create a rule to move it to a folder.
Look in each label once and move anything misfiled back. Ask your AI assistant to adjust the rule if something keeps landing in the wrong place.

example: Receipts | from: orders@, receipts@, subject 'your order' | skip inbox. Newsletters | from: hello@freshbakes.co, news@runclub.org | skip inbox. Notifications | from: no-reply@ | skip inbox. Travel | subject 'booking confirmation' | keep in inbox.
tips: Start with skipping the inbox only for senders you're sure about; you can always widen it later.
Gmail's built-in Promotions and Updates tabs already do some of this, so build on them rather than fighting them.

trigger.detail: Any new email arrives

actions.detail: Decide if it is a receipt, newsletter, notification, travel or personal
Apply the matching label and archive if it is low priority

t: Keep every invoice and receipt in one tidy place
d: Have invoice emails labelled as they arrive, then turn them into a monthly spreadsheet of supplier, date and amount in minutes.
when: Set up once, then at the end of each month

steps.b: In Gmail, search for words like invoice OR receipt OR 'payment confirmation', then create a filter from that search that applies an 'Invoices' label. Outlook users can make a rule that moves them to an Invoices folder.
At month end, open the label and save each PDF to a Google Drive or OneDrive folder named by month, such as 'Invoices 2026-11'.
Upload the PDFs (or paste the email text) into your AI assistant with this prompt. Remove bank details first if they're not needed.
steps.p: Extract the following from each invoice or receipt I've attached: supplier name, invoice number, invoice date (DD/MM/YYYY), due date if shown, amount before tax, tax, total, currency, and a one-word category from this list: [e.g. Software, Travel, Supplies, Utilities, Other]. Return a table with one row per document, in date order. If a value isn't on the document, write 'not shown' rather than guessing.

steps.b: Copy the table into a Google Sheet or Excel file with one tab per month, and spot-check the totals against two or three originals.

example: 02/11/2026 | Brightline Hosting | INV-2231 | £18.00 | VAT £3.60 | £21.60 | Software. 05/11/2026 | Kettle & Co Stationers | 8841 | £42.50 | VAT £8.50 | £51.00 | Supplies.
tips: Always check AI-extracted amounts against the original before using them for tax or accounts, and ask your accountant if you're unsure how to categorise something.
If you use Xero or QuickBooks, they have their own email-in addresses for bills that may save you this step.

trigger.detail: An email with an invoice or receipt arrives

actions.detail: Label it Invoices
Save the attachment to this month's invoices folder
Pull supplier, date, invoice number and totals
Add a row to the invoices spreadsheet

t: Catch up on a long email thread in a minute
d: Turn a 30-message thread into a short summary of what was decided, what's still open and what's expected of you.
when: When you're copied into a thread late or come back from leave

steps.b: Gemini in Gmail and Copilot in Outlook can summarise a thread from a button at the top of the email, if your plan includes it.
Open the thread, expand all messages, select all and copy. Check your workplace AI policy before pasting work emails into a personal AI account.
Paste the thread into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p:
Summarise this email thread for me. I am [your name and role]. Give me: 1) The background in two sentences. 2) Decisions already made, with who made them. 3) Open questions still being discussed. 4) Anything anyone has asked me or my team to do, with deadlines. 5) A suggested one-paragraph reply if one is needed from me. Use bullet points and keep it under 200 words.

Thread:
[paste thread]

example: Background: Venue for the 12 Dec staff lunch. Decided: The Old Mill, 40 people (Jo). Open: vegetarian numbers, who pays deposit. Asked of you: confirm final headcount by Fri 21 Nov. Suggested reply: 'Thanks all, I'll send the final headcount by Friday.'
tips: Ask 'what did I miss that sounds urgent?' as a follow-up question; it often surfaces a buried request.

trigger.detail: User opens a long thread and asks for a catch-up

actions.detail: Summarise background, decisions, open questions and asks
Draft a short reply if one is needed

t: Follow up on emails nobody has answered
d: Never lose track of unanswered emails: get reminded after a few days and send a friendly nudge that actually gets a reply.
when: Three working days after an important email goes unanswered

steps.h: Set a reminder when you send
steps.b: In Gmail, snooze your sent email or turn on Nudges in settings so it reappears if there's no reply. In Outlook, flag the sent message with a follow-up date.

steps.h: When it comes back, draft a nudge
steps.b: Paste your original email into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p:
I sent the email below [number] days ago to [who they are] and haven't had a reply. Write a short, friendly follow-up under 60 words that: doesn't sound annoyed, restates the one thing I need from them, makes it easy to answer (offer a yes/no or two options), and gives a gentle date. Give me two versions: one casual, one more formal.

Original email:
[paste email]

steps.b: Send the nudge as a reply to your original email so they have the context, and set another reminder for a week later.

example: Hi Lena, just floating this back to the top of your inbox. Could you let me know by Thursday whether the 3pm slot works? A quick yes or no is perfect. Thanks, Ali
tips: A specific question gets more replies than 'just checking in'.
If two nudges get nothing, try a different channel, like a quick call.

trigger.detail: Daily check for sent emails with no reply after 3 working days

actions.detail: Write a short, friendly follow-up
Save it as a draft reply in the original thread
Tell the user a nudge is ready to review

t: Build a set of ready-made replies you can reuse
d: Get polished templates for the emails you write over and over, saved in Gmail or Outlook and ready in two clicks.
when: Once, then add to it whenever you write the same email twice

steps.b: Think of the five emails you write most, such as sending prices, booking confirmations, saying you're running late, or declining a request.
Paste your list and an example of each (if you have one) into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write reusable email templates for these situations: [list your 5 situations]. I am [your role or business]. My tone is [e.g. friendly and professional]. For each template give: a short name, a subject line, and a body under 120 words with [SQUARE BRACKETS] for anything I need to fill in, such as [NAME] or [DATE]. Keep the language plain British English and end each with a clear next step.

steps.h: Turn on templates in your email app
steps.b: In Gmail, switch on Templates in settings (under Advanced), then save each draft as a template. In Outlook, use My Templates or Quick Parts to save them.
Insert a template, replace the brackets and send. If you keep changing the same sentence, update the saved template.

example: Name: Price list request. Subject: Our prices for [SERVICE]. Body: Hi [NAME], thanks for getting in touch. Our current prices are attached. Most clients choose [PACKAGE], which includes [WHAT'S INCLUDED]. Would you like to book a quick call this week to talk it through?
tips: Always do a final search for '[' before sending so no placeholders slip through.

trigger.detail: User asks for a set of templates

actions.detail: Write templates for each repeat situation
Save all templates in one reference document

t: Send personal-feeling emails to a whole list
d: Write one email, then send it to dozens of people from a spreadsheet, each with their name and a personal opening line.
when: For invitations, updates to clients or members, or event follow-ups

steps.b: In Google Sheets or Excel, make columns for first name, email address and a short note about each person (for example 'came to the June workshop').

steps.h: Ask AI for personal opening lines
steps.b: Copy the name and note columns only (not email addresses) into your AI assistant with this prompt, then paste the result back as a new column.
steps.p:
For each row below, write one friendly opening sentence (under 25 words) for an email about [your topic], referring naturally to the note. Don't overdo the flattery. Return a single column in the same order as the input, one line per row, with no numbering.

[paste names and notes]

steps.b: Draft the body in your email app or ask AI to help. Use placeholders that match your column names, such as {{First name}} and {{Opening}}.
Use Gmail's mail merge (available on some Google Workspace plans) or Word's Mailings tab with Outlook to send one email per row. Send a test to yourself first.
Add a 'Replied' column to your sheet and tick people off as they respond, so you know who to follow up.

example: Row: Hannah | came to the June workshop. Opening: 'It was lovely to meet you at the June workshop, and I hope the planning templates have been useful.' Email: Hi Hannah, It was lovely to meet you... We're running a follow-up session on 4 Dec.
tips: Only email people who've agreed to hear from you, and for marketing include an easy way to opt out.
Check your provider's daily sending limits before sending to a big list; Mailchimp may suit larger lists better.

trigger.detail: A contact is added to the mailing sheet

actions.detail: Write a personal opening line from the note
Save the opening line in the row
Create a personalised email for review before sending

t: Turn a rambling draft into a short, clear email
d: Paste a messy draft and get back a tidy email with the main point first, short paragraphs and one clear ask.
when: Before sending anything long or important

steps.b: Type everything you want to say without worrying about order or wording. Bullet points are fine.
Paste your draft with this prompt.
steps.p:
Rewrite my draft email so it's clear and quick to read. Rules: put the main point or request in the first two sentences; keep it under [150] words; use short paragraphs; keep every fact, date and number exactly as I wrote them; don't add anything new; match a [friendly / formal] tone. Suggest a subject line under 8 words. Then list any part of my draft that was unclear so I can fix it.

Draft:
[paste draft]

steps.b: Read the new version against your notes to make sure nothing important was dropped, then send.

example: Subject: Need your sign-off on the new rota by Friday. Hi team, I need everyone's sign-off on the December rota by Friday 28 Nov. The main change is late shifts now finish at 9pm, not 10pm. Please reply 'OK' or let me know which dates clash.
tips: Ask for a version with bullet points if your reader is skimming on a phone.

trigger.detail: User pastes a draft and asks for a rewrite

actions.detail: Rewrite the draft with the main point first
Replace the draft with the clearer version

t: Check if a suspicious email is a scam
d: Get a plain-English verdict on a worrying email, with the warning signs spelled out and what to do next.
when: Whenever an email asks you to click, pay or log in

steps.b: Leave links and attachments alone. Copy the sender's full address (not just the display name), the subject and the text.

steps.h: Ask AI for a second opinion
steps.b: Paste the details with this prompt. Never paste passwords or codes.
steps.p: Help me check whether this email is likely to be a phishing scam. Sender address: [full address]. Subject: [subject]. Text: [paste text]. Link text shown (don't visit it): [paste if any]. Give me: 1) A verdict: likely scam, unclear, or likely genuine. 2) Each warning sign you can see, explained in plain English. 3) What I should do now. 4) How to check with the real organisation safely, without using any contact details in the email.

steps.b: If it looks like a scam, report it using the 'Report phishing' or 'Report' option in Gmail or Outlook, then delete it. If unsure, contact the organisation using a number or website you already know.

example: Verdict: likely scam. Signs: sender is 'support@royalmaii-parcels.com' (misspelt), urgent 'pay £1.99 within 24 hours', generic greeting, link text doesn't match the company. Next: report as phishing, delete, and check any real parcel on the courier's own app.
tips: AI can't see where a link really goes, so treat 'likely genuine' as a hint, not a guarantee.
At work, forward suspicious emails to your IT team as well.

trigger.detail: User flags an email as suspicious

actions.detail: Rate the email as likely scam, unclear or likely genuine
Explain the warning signs and safe next steps
Show the verdict to the user

t: Clear out newsletters you never read
d: End up with a short list of newsletters worth keeping and a quick plan to unsubscribe from the rest.
when: Once a quarter

steps.b: In Gmail, look for 'Manage subscriptions' in the left menu if your account has it, or search for the word unsubscribe. In Outlook, search for unsubscribe and sort by sender.
Write down or copy the sender names and roughly how often they arrive.
Paste your list into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Here's a list of newsletters and marketing emails I get, with how often: [paste list]. What I care about right now: [e.g. local events, my running club, deals on kids' clothes]. Sort them into three groups: Keep (useful and I'd miss it), Keep but filter out of my inbox (occasionally useful), and Unsubscribe. Give one short reason for each. Put the Unsubscribe list first.

steps.b: Use the unsubscribe link at the top of each email in Gmail or Outlook. For the 'filter' group, set up a filter or rule to send them to a Reading label or folder.

example: Unsubscribe (14): Shoe outlet daily deals, three old webinar lists, travel site you used once. Keep but filter (6): supermarket offers, two shops. Keep (4): Running club news, local library events, school newsletter, Sunday book review.
tips: Only use unsubscribe links from brands you recognise; for spammy senders, mark as spam instead.

trigger.detail: First Saturday of every quarter

actions.detail: Sort newsletter senders into keep, filter and unsubscribe
Send the unsubscribe list to the user

t: Get one weekly digest of all your newsletters
d: Newsletters skip your inbox all week, then on Sunday you get one short digest of the best bits with links to read more.
when: Every Sunday

steps.h: Route newsletters to a Reading label
steps.b: Create a Gmail filter (or Outlook rule) for your newsletter senders that applies a 'Reading' label or moves them to a Reading folder, skipping the inbox.
On Sunday, open the Reading label, select the week's emails and copy their text, or forward them to yourself as one email.
Paste them into your AI assistant with this prompt. If your assistant is connected to your email, ask it to read the Reading label directly.
steps.p:
Make me a weekly digest from these newsletters. My interests: [your interests]. For each newsletter give: its name, the 1 to 3 items most relevant to me in one line each, and mark anything time-sensitive (events, sales ending, deadlines) with 'DATE:'. Finish with 'Worth reading in full' listing at most 2 issues and why. Skip adverts and sponsored sections.

[paste newsletters]

steps.b: Paste the digest into your notes app, add any dates to your calendar, then archive the week's newsletters in one go.

example: Garden Notes: plant garlic before mid-Dec; frost-proof pot guide. Town Events: DATE: Christmas market Sat 6 Dec. Money Weekly: energy price cap changes in Jan. Worth reading in full: Garden Notes, for the bulb planting calendar.
tips: Ask it to say 'nothing new this week' for a newsletter rather than padding the digest.

trigger.detail: Sundays at 9am

actions.detail: Summarise the week's newsletters by the user's interests
Add any dated events found
Send the digest to the user

t: Write an out-of-office reply that helps people
d: Get a clear, friendly out-of-office message with your return date, who to contact and what will wait, ready to switch on.
when: Before any holiday, leave or busy period

steps.b: Note your away dates, the date you'll reply by, who covers urgent matters and how to reach them.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Write an out-of-office email reply. I'm away from [date] to [date] and will reply from [date]. For urgent [topics], contact [name, role, email]. Things that can wait: [e.g. invoices, general questions]. Audience: [clients / colleagues / both]. Keep it under 70 words, warm but businesslike, no jokes. Also give me a shorter 25-word version for internal colleagues.

steps.b: In Gmail, find Vacation responder in settings and set the first and last day. In Outlook, use Automatic replies and tick the option to send only during a time range.

example: Thanks for your email. I'm away until Monday 5 January and will reply by Wednesday 7th. For anything urgent about orders, please contact Maya Patel (Customer Team) at orders@example.com. Everything else will be waiting safely for me.
tips: Set the reply to start the evening before you leave so late messages get it too.
Avoid saying exactly where you are or that your home is empty.

trigger.detail: A holiday or leave event is added to the calendar

actions.detail: Write an out-of-office reply with dates and cover contact
Remind the user to switch it on the day before

t: Answer customer enquiries faster with your own FAQ
d: Build an AI helper that knows your prices, policies and tone, so drafting a reply to any enquiry takes seconds.
when: Whenever a customer emails a question

steps.b: In a Google Doc or Word file, list your prices, opening hours, delivery or booking rules, refund policy and the ten questions you're asked most, with your usual answers.
Make a ChatGPT custom GPT, a Claude Project or a Gemini Gem (whichever you use), upload your answer sheet and paste these instructions.
steps.p: You help me reply to customer emails for [business name], a [type of business]. Only use facts from the attached answer sheet. When I paste a customer email: 1) Write a friendly reply under 120 words in British English, signed [your name]. 2) If the answer isn't in the sheet, say 'NOT IN SHEET' and suggest what I should find out, rather than guessing. 3) Below the reply, list any upsell or next step that would genuinely help the customer.

steps.h: Paste enquiries in as they arrive
steps.b: Copy the customer's question (leave out their address or card details) into your helper, check the draft and send it from your email.

steps.h: Keep the sheet up to date
steps.b: Whenever you answer something new, add it to the answer sheet and re-upload it so the helper learns it.

example: Customer: Do you deliver to Hove on Saturdays? Draft: Hi Chris, yes, we deliver to Hove on Saturdays between 9am and 1pm. Orders need to be in by 6pm Thursday, and delivery is free over £40. Would you like me to reserve a slot for you? Best, Jen
tips: Never paste payment details or full addresses; the helper doesn't need them to draft a reply.
Check every reply before sending, especially anything about refunds or prices.

trigger.detail: A customer enquiry arrives

actions.detail: Check the question is covered by the answer sheet
Draft a reply using only facts from the answer sheet
Save the reply as a draft for review

t: Turn emails into a clear to-do list
d: Get every request buried in your inbox pulled into one list with deadlines, then sent straight to your task app.
when: At the end of each working day

steps.b: As you read, star emails in Gmail or flag them in Outlook. Flagged Outlook emails show up in Microsoft To Do, and in Gmail you can use 'Add to Tasks' from the email menu.
At day's end, copy the starred or flagged emails into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p:
Read these emails and list every task I need to do. For each give: the task starting with a verb, who it's for, the deadline (or 'no deadline'), and a time estimate (5 min, 30 min, 1 hr+). Merge duplicates. Sort by deadline, then by quickest first. Put anything that just needs a one-line reply in a separate 'Quick replies' list at the top.

[paste emails]

steps.h: Add them to your task app
steps.b: Copy the list into Google Tasks, Microsoft To Do, Reminders or your notes app, adding the deadlines as due dates.
Unstar or unflag the emails once they're on your list so your inbox shows only new things.

example: Quick replies: Confirm Tues lunch with Ola. Tasks: Send updated quote to Greenway Builders - Fri 14 Nov - 30 min. Book van MOT - by 20 Nov - 5 min. Review draft brochure from Leo - no deadline - 1 hr+.
tips: Anything taking under two minutes, just do it now instead of listing it.

actions.detail: Pull tasks, deadlines and time estimates from flagged emails
Add each task to the user's to-do list with its due date
Remove the flag once a task is added

t: Say no politely without damaging the relationship
d: Get a kind, clear email that turns down a request, invite or extra work while keeping the door open where you want it.
when: When you need to decline something

steps.b: Work out if there's anything you can offer, such as a later date, a smaller version or a recommendation. It's fine if the answer is nothing.
Paste the request and this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Help me say no to this request: [paste or describe the request]. Who it's from: [relationship]. My real reason (you decide how much to share): [reason]. What I can offer instead, if anything: [alternative or 'nothing']. Write a reply under 90 words that thanks them, says no clearly in the first two sentences, doesn't over-apologise or make up excuses, and ends warmly. Give me one version that keeps the door open and one that closes it kindly.

steps.b: A quick, clear no is kinder than a slow maybe. Send it today if you can.

example: Hi Gemma, thank you for thinking of me for the committee. I'm not able to take it on this year, as my evenings are full until the summer. I'd be happy to help with the spring fair on the day if that's useful. Wishing you a great first meeting!
tips: Remove 'just', 'sorry' and 'I'm afraid' from the final version; one thank-you is enough.

trigger.detail: User asks for help declining a request

actions.detail: Write a door-open and a door-closed decline
Save the chosen version as a reply draft

t: Send instant replies to common enquiries automatically
d: Enquiries with set keywords get an instant helpful reply, are labelled for you and land in a weekly list of who to follow up.
when: Whenever a new enquiry email arrives

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant to draft short replies for your two or three most common enquiries.
steps.p: I run [business]. Write auto-reply emails for these common enquiries: [e.g. price requests, availability, opening hours]. Each must: thank them, answer the basics in under 100 words using these facts: [paste facts], say a real person will follow up within [time frame] if needed, and include a link placeholder [BOOKING LINK]. steps.b: Turn on Templates in Gmail's settings (under Advanced), then paste each reply into a new email and save it as a template.

steps.h: Create a filter that replies for you
steps.b: Search Gmail for the words that identify each enquiry (for example sent to your contact address with 'price' in the subject), create a filter from the search, and choose to send the template and apply a label such as 'Enquiry - Prices'.

steps.h: Test before you rely on it
steps.b: Send yourself an email from another account using the trigger words, and check the reply arrives and reads well.

steps.h: Write your reply in your own words
steps.b: Type what you want to say in English, as naturally as you would to anyone.

t: Get a 2-minute summary of every meeting
d: Finish each video call with a short summary of what was discussed, what was decided and who's doing what, without taking notes.
when: After every video meeting

steps.b: Use Zoom AI Companion's meeting summary, Google Meet's 'Take notes for me' or Teams Copilot's recap, if your plan includes it. Tell attendees at the start that notes are being taken.
If you don't have an AI note-taker, turn on transcription or captions where available and download or copy the transcript after the call.
Paste the transcript or the app's own notes into your AI assistant with this prompt. Remove anything confidential first and follow your workplace AI policy.
steps.p:
Summarise this meeting transcript. Meeting: [title], attendees: [names]. Give me: 1) Three-sentence summary. 2) Decisions made. 3) Action items as a table: task, owner, deadline (write 'not set' if none was agreed). 4) Open questions to carry to next time. Use only what was actually said; don't invent owners or dates.

Transcript:
[paste]

steps.b: Paste the summary into the meeting chat, a shared doc or an email to attendees within the hour.

example: Summary: Agreed the spring newsletter goes out 3 March with 4 articles. Decisions: drop the printed version. Actions: Write intro - Kemi - 20 Feb. Gather photos - Dan - 24 Feb. Book printer quote - not set. Open: who approves final copy?

Check everyone is comfortable being recorded, especially with external guests.

If an owner or deadline is unclear, mark it '?' so I can check. 2) Write a follow-up email to the attendees under 150 words: thank them, recap the 2 or 3 main decisions, list the actions, and confirm the next meeting date [date if known]. Notes:
[paste notes]

steps.b: Replace any '?' with the right name or date, then send the email from your usual account.

example: Actions: Rachel - send venue options - Fri 21 Nov. Imran - get catering quotes - ?. Me - draft invite - Mon 24 Nov. Email: Hi all, thanks for a productive chat today. We agreed on a Thursday evening event for around 60 people...

t: Walk into any meeting prepared in ten minutes

steps.b: Open the calendar invite and copy the title, description and attendee roles. Add any related email or document text, removing anything confidential.
Paste it all into your AI assistant with this prompt.
steps.p: Help me prepare for a meeting. Details: [paste invite and background]. My role: [your role]. What I want from it: [your goal]. Give me a one-page brief: 1) The likely purpose of the meeting in one sentence. 2) Three key facts I should have to hand. 3) Five good questions to ask, most important first. 4) Two possible objections or tricky questions and short answers. 5) The single outcome I should push for, phrased as a sentence I can say at the end.

steps.h: Keep it on screen or paper
steps.b: Paste the brief into the calendar event's notes so it's there when the meeting starts.

example: Purpose: Agree next year's cleaning contract terms. Key facts: current cost £640/month; two missed visits in Oct. Ask first: 'What can you guarantee on missed visits?' Push for: 'Can we confirm a 12-month contract with a service credit for any missed visit?'

actions.detail: Create a one-page prep brief from the invite and background
Send the brief to the user

t: Write a meeting agenda people will actually follow
d: Get a timed agenda with a clear purpose, the decisions needed and what to read beforehand, ready to paste into the invite.
when: When you're sending a meeting invite

steps.b: Note the topics, how long the meeting is, and anything that must be decided by the end.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Create an agenda for a [length]-minute meeting about [topic] with [who's attending]. Topics: [list]. Decisions we need by the end: [list]. Format: a one-line purpose at the top; then each item with minutes allowed, who leads it, and whether it's 'Inform', 'Discuss' or 'Decide'; finish with 5 minutes to confirm actions. Keep items in a sensible order, put decisions early, and tell me if there's too much for the time.

steps.b: Paste the agenda into the invite description and attach or link any pre-reading.

example: Purpose: Choose a date and format for the summer fete. 1. Budget update - 5 min - Ana - Inform. 2. Pick date (21 Jun or 28 Jun) - 10 min - Chair - Decide. 3. Stall ideas - 10 min - All - Discuss. 4. Volunteers needed - 5 min - Tom - Discuss. 5. Confirm actions - 5 min.
tips: If the AI says it won't fit, cut an item or make it a written update rather than going over time.

trigger.detail: User creates a meeting with no description

actions.detail: Draft a timed agenda from the topics
Add the agenda to the invite description

t: Find a meeting time that works across time zones
d: Get three sensible meeting slots for people in different countries, with each person's local time shown side by side.
when: When you're arranging a call with people abroad

steps.h: Note who's where and when they're free
steps.b: List each person's city and the rough hours they're available, plus your own free times this week.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Find meeting times for a [length]-minute call between: [name - city - available hours, for each person]. Dates: [date range]. Avoid times before 8am or after 7pm local for anyone where possible. Suggest the 3 best slots and show a table with each person's local date and time. Flag if any slot falls on a public holiday or weekend in any of the countries, and note any clock changes in that period.

steps.b: Use Google Calendar's 'Find a time' or Outlook's Scheduling Assistant to confirm the slot is clear, then send the invite. The calendar shows it in each person's own time zone.

example: Option 1: Tue 18 Nov - London 9:00, Toronto 4:00 (too early), Dubai 13:00. Option 2: Tue 18 Nov - London 14:00, Toronto 9:00, Dubai 18:00 (best). Option 3: Wed 19 Nov - London 15:00, Toronto 10:00, Dubai 19:00.
tips: AI can get clock changes wrong, so check times against your calendar before sending.
Rotate awkward early or late slots fairly if you meet regularly.

actions.detail: Suggest 3 slots with local times for each person
Create the invite for the chosen slot

t: Let people book time with you without the back-and-forth
d: Share one booking link so clients or colleagues pick a free slot themselves, with a clear page explaining what each meeting is for.
when: Set up once, share whenever someone asks to meet

steps.b: Use Google Calendar's appointment schedules, Outlook's Bookings if your plan includes it, or Calendly's free plan. Each connects to your calendar so booked slots are blocked out.

steps.h: Write your booking page with AI
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant to get the wording.
steps.p: I'm setting up an online booking page for [your service or role]. Meeting types: [e.g. 15-min intro call, 45-min consultation]. For each, write: a clear name, a 2-sentence description of who it's for and what happens, what to prepare, and up to 3 short questions to ask when booking (e.g. 'What would you like to cover?'). Also write a one-line confirmation message. Friendly, plain British English.

steps.b: Choose the hours you're bookable, add buffer time between meetings, set a minimum notice period and limit how many bookings you'll take per day.
Add the link to your email signature, website or replies, then book a test slot yourself to check it works.

example: 15-minute intro call: A quick chat to see if we're a good fit for your garden project. Bring a few photos of the space. Booking question: 'What would you like help with?' Confirmation: 'Thanks, you're booked in! I'll call you on the number you gave.'
tips: A 15-minute buffer after each meeting stops your day becoming back-to-back.

trigger.detail: Someone books a slot on the booking page

actions.detail: Add the booking to the calendar
Send a confirmation with what to prepare
Summarise the booker's answers into prep notes

t: Get your day's meetings and prep notes every morning
d: Wake up to an email listing today's meetings, then turn it into a short plan with prep tasks and gaps for focused work.
when: Every weekday morning

steps.h: Turn on your daily agenda email
steps.b: In Google Calendar's settings, find the notification options for your calendar and switch on the daily agenda email. Outlook users can connect their AI assistant to the calendar or copy the day view instead.

steps.h: Connect your assistant if you can
steps.b: Gemini with Google Workspace, Copilot in Outlook, or ChatGPT and Claude with a Google Calendar connector can read your calendar directly, if your plan includes it.
Paste the agenda email (or ask your connected assistant) with this prompt.
steps.p: Here's my calendar for today: [paste agenda or 'read my calendar for today']. My top priority today is [priority]. Give me: 1) A timeline of the day with meetings and free gaps. 2) For each meeting, one line on what to prepare and how long it will take. 3) The best gap for focused work on my priority. 4) Any clashes, back-to-backs with no break, or meetings missing a video link or location. Keep it under 200 words.

steps.b: Create a recurring 10-minute calendar event at the start of each day called 'Plan today', with the prompt pasted in its description.

example: 9:30 Team stand-up (prep: nothing). 11:00 Supplier call (prep: check last invoice, 5 min). Gap 12:00-14:00: best time for the funding report. 14:00 and 15:00 back-to-back: leave 5 min early. 16:00 Interview: no video link yet, check with HR.
tips: If your plan doesn't include connectors, the daily agenda email plus copy and paste works just as well.

trigger.detail: Weekdays at 7:30am

actions.detail: Read today's calendar events
Build a day plan with prep tasks, focus gaps and clashes
Send the plan to the user

t: Find out where your week's time really goes
d: Get a breakdown of your calendar by type of meeting, plus three practical changes to win back a few hours a week.
when: Once a month

steps.h: Copy two weeks of your calendar
steps.b: Switch to the week or schedule view and copy or screenshot the last two weeks, including meeting titles and times.
Paste or attach it with this prompt. Shorten any sensitive meeting titles first.
steps.p: Analyse my calendar for the last two weeks: [paste or attach]. My working hours are [hours]. My most important goals right now are [goals]. Give me: 1) Hours spent per category (1:1s, team meetings, external, admin, focus time, other) in a table. 2) Recurring meetings that could be shorter, less frequent or replaced by a written update. 3) The longest stretch of free time each day. 4) Three specific changes I could make next week, with the hours each would save.

steps.b: Pick the easiest suggestion, such as shortening a recurring meeting from 60 to 30 minutes, and change it in your calendar today.

example: Team meetings: 9.5 hrs. 1:1s: 4 hrs. External: 3 hrs. Focus time: 2 hrs. Suggestions: make Friday wrap-up a written update (saves 1 hr); shorten weekly ops to 30 min (saves 2 hrs over 2 weeks); block Tue and Thu 9-11 as focus time.
tips: Google Calendar's Time Insights panel and Outlook's Viva Insights (if available) give you similar numbers automatically.

trigger.detail: First Monday of every month

actions.detail: Read the last two weeks of calendar events
Group events into meeting categories
Suggest three changes to free up time
Send the audit to the user

t: Protect time for focused work every week
d: Set up recurring focus blocks in your calendar that decline clashing meetings, sized and placed to suit how you work.
when: Set up once, review monthly

steps.b: Ask your AI assistant to help you decide where focus time should go.
steps.p: Help me plan weekly focus time. My usual meetings: [e.g. Mon 10am team, Wed 2pm 1:1s]. My best concentration time: [e.g. mornings]. Work I need deep focus for: [tasks]. Suggest 3 to 4 recurring focus blocks per week, each 90 minutes to 2 hours, avoiding my meetings. Give each a clear name that tells colleagues what I'm doing, and a one-line note for the event description explaining how to reach me if it's urgent.

steps.b: In Google Calendar, choose 'Focus time' as the event type if your account has it, which can auto-decline meetings. In Outlook, create a recurring event marked as Busy, or use Viva Insights focus time if your plan includes it.
Turn on Do Not Disturb on your phone and computer during the blocks, and pause chat notifications in Slack or Teams.

example: Tue 9:00-11:00 Focus: quarterly report. Thu 9:00-11:00 Focus: client proposals. Fri 13:30-15:00 Focus: planning next week. Description: 'Heads-down time. For anything urgent, call me on my mobile.'
tips: Treat focus blocks like a meeting with your most important client: move them, don't delete them.

Add the focus blocks to the calendar

steps.b: Use your phone's voice recorder app. Ask permission before recording anyone else, and keep the phone close to whoever is speaking.
Many phone recorder apps now transcribe automatically. If yours doesn't, upload the audio file to ChatGPT or Gemini, which can work with audio on many plans.
Paste the transcript or attach the recording with this prompt.
steps.p:
Turn this recording transcript into clear notes. Context: [e.g. meeting with landlord about repairs]. Give me: 1) A title and date line. 2) Key points as bullets, grouped by topic. 3) Anything agreed, with who agreed it. 4) Next steps with owners and dates. 5) Any numbers, prices or dates mentioned, listed separately so I can check them. Don't add anything that wasn't said.

[paste transcript]

steps.b: Paste the notes into your notes app or a shared doc, and add any dates to your calendar.

tips: Always get consent before recording others, and delete recordings once you have your notes if they contain personal details.

Ask your AI assistant for a structure you can copy for each meeting.
steps.p: Create a simple template for a recurring [weekly / fortnightly] one-to-one between [role] and [role]. Include sections for: wins since last time, topics from each person, blockers, feedback both ways, actions with owners and dates, and one 'bigger picture' question that rotates each week. Give me 8 rotating bigger-picture questions too. Keep headings short.

steps.b: Attach the doc to the recurring calendar event so both of you can add topics during the week.
Once a month, paste the last four meetings into your AI assistant and ask for themes, repeated blockers and actions that haven't been done.

Remind both people to add topics

steps.h: Find scheduled tasks in your assistant

steps.h: Ask AI for the card list
steps.b: Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I'm setting up a project board for [project]. Team: [names and roles]. Deadline: [date]. Give me a list of 15 to 25 cards. Each card is one line in this format: [task starting with a verb] - [owner] - [due date]. Group them under these list headings: Backlog, This week, Waiting on others. steps.b: Make a new Trello board or a Notion board database with the lists Backlog, This week, Doing, Waiting on others and Done.

tips: Limit 'Doing' to two or three cards per person; it keeps work flowing instead of half-done.

t: Get started on a task you keep putting off

when: When you've been avoiding something for days

steps.h: Be honest about what's stopping you
steps.b: Note the task and why it feels hard: boring, confusing, scary, or too big.
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: I keep putting off this task: [task]. It feels hard because [reason]. Help me start. Give me: 1) A first step so small it takes under 2 minutes. 2) A 25-minute plan broken into 3 or 4 mini steps. 3) What 'good enough' looks like for a first attempt. 4) One reframe for why this feels hard, in a kind, practical tone, not a pep talk.

steps.b: Do the 2-minute step straight away, then start a timer on your phone and work through the mini steps. Stop when it rings if you want to.

example: 2-minute step: Open the tax return website and log in. 25 minutes: 1) Find last year's P60 (5 min). 2) Fill in personal details (5 min). 3) Enter income figures (10 min). 4) Save and note questions (5 min). Good enough: Half done and saved.
tips: Starting is the hardest part; most people keep going once the first step is done.

steps.h: Ask AI to design the sheet

t: Make a tough decision with a clear comparison
d: Lay out your options and get a simple scoring table, the trade-offs in plain words and questions to settle what matters most.
when: When you're stuck between two or more choices

steps.b: List each option and what you know about it, plus what you care about most (cost, time, stress, family, growth).
Paste this prompt into your AI assistant.
steps.p: Help me decide between these options: [list options with key facts]. What matters to me, in order: [your priorities]. 1) Ask me up to 3 questions first if anything important is missing. 2) Then make a table scoring each option 1 to 5 on each priority, weighted by my order, with a total. 3) Describe the biggest trade-off of each option in one sentence. 4) Tell me what would have to be true for each option to be the right one. steps.b: Read the results the next morning. If the top score feels wrong, that tells you something about what you really want.

example: Options: Job A (more pay, 1hr commute) vs Job B (less pay, hybrid). Weighted totals: A 31, B 36. Trade-off A: £6k more but 10 hrs a week travelling. B is right if flexibility for school pick-ups matters more than savings this year.
tips: For big money, health or legal decisions, use this to clarify your thinking, then check with a qualified professional.

steps.p: You are my personal planning assistant. Use the attached 'about me' page for context.
